newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy expanding, prices subdued, Fed says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy expanding, prices subdued, Fed says.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The economy grew moderately the past two months with wages and retail prices mostly subdued, the Federal Reserve said on Wednesday.

In its latest summary of national economic activity, the central bank painted a picture of an economy almost too good to be true -- still growing six years into an expansion with few, if any, signs of inflation.
"(The economy) generally continued to expand at a moderate rate through March and April," the Fed said in its Beige Book, so named for the colour of its cover.

The report comes about two weeks before Fed policy-makers meet on May 20 to decide whether to raise interest rates again. The Fed raised short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years in a bid to keep the economy from overheating and inflation from rising.
"The question to be decided is should we make another (move) or have we done enough," Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin told CNBC television.
Analysts are divided over whether the central bank will raise rates again this month, and the Beige Book did little to clear up the uncertainty.

The Fed said labour markets across the country remained tight, with employers reporting shortages of qualified help. But so far, that has not shown up in any big surge in wages that could portend higher inflation ahead.
"Despite tight labour markets, upward wage pressures remained generally subdued," the Fed said.

The government said last week that economic growth jumped to a 5.6 percent rate in the first quarter, the strongest in nine years, and that the unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent in April, the lowest since 1973, though job growth was modest. Neither report indicated a sharp pickup in inflation.

In a separate report Wednesday, the Labour Department said workers enjoyed their biggest increase in compensation in the first quarter in five years. But that did not raise costs much for employers because worker productivity also grew.

Productivity grew at an annual rate of 2 percent in the first quarter, the fastest rate in more than three years and nearly double the fourth quarter's 1.1 percent pace. Worker compensation soared 4.7 percent, but firms' labour costs rose a more modest 2.7 percent, thanks to the higher productivity.
The bond market nevertheless fell on the Labour Department report as productivity grew less than Wall Street had expected given the surge in economic growth in the first quarter.
Productivity often jumps when the economy soars as employers ask existing workers to put in more overtime rather than hiring more workers.

Hurt also by weak bidding at an auction of 10-year Treasury notes, the key 30-year Treasury bond fell 29/32, or $9.06 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield to 6.96 percent from 6.89 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The bond market's weakness helped drag down stocks, with the Dow Jones industrial average falling 139.67 to 7,085.65.
In its Beige Book, the Fed said the housing and construction industries remained strong and that manufacturers continued to run their businesses at very high levels.
The economy's strength, though, has not put much upward pressure on consumer prices, the report said.
"Prices at the retail level remained subdued," it said.
Analysts said the report signalled price pressures were growing but not yet bubbling through in the form of higher inflation that could undermine the economic expansion.

"The most recent evidence justifies another modest tightening of credit by the Fed, but I don't think there is any urgency," said David Jones, vice chairman of Wall Street broker Aubrey G. Lanston and Co.
The Beige Book is issued by the Fed eight times a year and is based on reports from its 12 district banks. The latest one was based on interviews with businesses before April 28.
